question: What is the medical term for difficulty swallowing?
explanation: Dysphagia is the clinical term used when a patient experiences trouble moving food or liquid from the mouth to the stomach safely. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T7#GNS112_U5_T7_h1)

question: Which little flap of tissue automatically covers your windpipe when you swallow, keeping food out of your lungs?
explanation: Think of the epiglottis as a trapdoor! When you swallow, it folds down over your larynx and trachea to block food and drinks from taking a wrong turn into your lungs.

question: What is the main danger when food or liquid silently slips into a patient's lungs without them even coughing?
explanation: When foreign material and mouth bacteria sneak down into the lungs, they set up camp and cause a nasty infection known as aspiration pneumonia. Always stay alert!

question: Your patient just took a sip of water and now sounds wet and gurgling when they speak. What is your very first nursing move?

options.A: Document normal finding and continue the meal
options.B: Stop feeding immediately and assess the airway
options.C: Encourage the patient to talk more to clear the voice
options.D: Offer a thicker fluid to clear the throat

explanation: That wet voice is a red flag telling you liquid has hit the vocal cords! Stop the meal right away to protect your patient from choking or lung infections.

question: What is the best bed position to set a patient in before you feed them?
explanation: Sitting them straight up (High Fowler's at 90 degrees) lets gravity do the hard work, pulling food safely down the esophagus instead of toward the airway.

question: Why should you keep a patient sitting upright for about 30 to 60 minutes after they finish eating?

options.A: To encourage active digestion and prevent constipation
options.B: To prevent gastric reflux and subsequent aspiration
options.C: To allow the nurse time to chart the intake accurately
options.D: To improve nutrient absorption in the small intestine

explanation: Gravity is your best friend here! Keeping them upright stops food and stomach acid from creeping back up into the throat while digestion gets started.

question: How does tucking the chin down to the chest help a patient who has trouble swallowing?

options.A: It narrows the airway entrance to protect the lungs
options.B: It relaxes the jaw muscles during heavy chewing
options.C: It opens the lower esophageal sphincter faster
options.D: It increases saliva production in the oral cavity

explanation: The chin-tuck is a neat trick! It physically shifts the throat structures to close off the windpipe, giving food a safer path to the stomach.

question: You are feeding a patient who looks very tired and worn out. What is the safest way to handle their meal?

options.A: Allowing frequent rest periods and offering smaller, more frequent meals
options.B: Laying the patient flat in bed to conserve their physical energy
options.C: Mixing all the food together so it is easier to swallow quickly
options.D: Feeding the remaining food much faster to finish on time

explanation: Tired muscles make swallowing mistakes easy. Pacing the meal and serving smaller portions keeps your patient safe and energized.

question: Which food texture is safest for a patient with severe swallowing difficulties and missing teeth?
explanation: Pureed foods are smooth and need zero chewing effort, making them much safer and easier for a struggling patient to swallow.

question: Why do speech therapists and nurses sometimes add thickeners to drinks for dysphagia patients?

options.A: They slow down the flow rate to allow airway closure time
options.B: They prevent the liquid from tasting bitter to the patient
options.C: They provide extra calories and protein for wound healing
options.D: They stimulate the taste buds to increase appetite

explanation: Thin liquids rush down a weak throat way too fast before the epiglottis can close. Thickening the drink slows it down just enough for a safe swallow!

question: What is an important nursing task to do right after a patient finishes eating to lower their risk of pneumonia?

options.B: Lowering the head of the bed completely
options.C: Offering a large glass of thin water

explanation: Brushing the teeth and cleaning the mouth clears away leftover food bits and bacteria that could otherwise slip into the lungs later.

question: Why is it smart to check inside a patient's mouth with a penlight after they finish a meal?

options.A: To check for leftover food pockets that could lead to aspiration
options.B: To ensure the patient has brushed their own teeth properly
options.C: To check if the patient's dentures need permanent resizing
options.D: To measure the exact pH of the remaining saliva

explanation: Patients with weak mouth muscles often hoard food in their cheeks. Finding and clearing those pockets prevents food from sliding into the airway later!
